opus-5.5.text:
I think the starting point is recognizing that the old bargain has broken. For twenty-plus years the web ran on an implicit deal: you let crawlers index your content, and in exchange you got traffic, and traffic you could monetize through ads or subscriptions. When an AI agent reads your page, synthesizes it, and hands the answer back to a user, that loop doesn't close. The value still gets created, but it doesn't flow back to whoever produced the content. So any workable model has to reconnect value to the source.

I'd point to a few properties it needs.

First, it has to be granular and machine-native. Agents are going to be the dominant consumers of the web, making enormous numbers of requests, often in the middle of a task. You can't have a human negotiating a licensing deal for each one. The pricing has to be expressed in a way an agent can read, understand, and act on in real time: this content costs this much, under these terms, for this kind of use.

Second, it has to distinguish between kinds of use. Pulling a page once to answer a live question is very different from ingesting an archive to train a model. Those deserve different prices, and publishers should be able to set them separately. Today it's mostly binary, you block the crawler or you don't, and that's too blunt.

Third, it has to work for the long tail, not just the big publishers who can sign bespoke deals with the large labs. If only the New York Times and a handful of others get paid, you've built something that concentrates the web even further. A small, high-quality, niche source should be able to participate just as easily.

Fourth, the economics have to make sense for the buyer as well. If access is too expensive or too unpredictable, agents route around it, they use worse sources or stale data, and quality suffers for everyone. So you want something like a market, where prices reflect how valuable and unique the content actually is, and where agents can make sensible decisions about what's worth paying for.

And finally there's trust: attribution, provenance, some verification that the content is what it claims to be and that terms were honored. Payment without accountability doesn't hold up.

If you get those pieces right, I think you end up with a healthier web than the ad-driven one, because you're paying for the content's actual usefulness rather than for how many eyeballs it captures. That's a better incentive to build around.

r001.rationale: It says prices should reflect content’s value and uniqueness and mentions high-quality sources, but does not clearly say pricing should vary with content quality.

r002.rationale: It calls for different prices for live answers and model training, but does not state that price should vary with the value of work performed using the same content.

r003.rationale: It calls for machine-readable, real-time pricing that agents can use without bespoke negotiations for each request, and says smaller sources should be able to participate.

r004.rationale: It discusses market incentives and trust, but does not identify participants’ willingness to collaborate as the test of incentive alignment.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest starting point is that the current model is broken in a way almost everyone agrees on but nobody has the right incentives to fix alone. The web was built on an implicit bargain: you let crawlers in, they send you traffic, you monetize that traffic. AI breaks the bargain because the answer gets delivered without the visit. So the question isn't really "how do we price access," it's "what replaces the traffic deal."

A few things I think a workable model needs.

First, it has to price usage, not crawling. The crawl itself is almost worthless. What matters is what happens downstream: did the content get used to answer a question, did it shape a response, was it the thing that made the answer good. If you charge per fetch, you end up with publishers blocking everything and models getting worse, which is bad for both sides. If you can attribute at the moment of use, you can pay for value at the moment it's created.

Second, it has to be machine-negotiable. There are hundreds of millions of sites and, soon, millions of agents. No one is signing bilateral licensing deals at that scale. The deals you've seen between the big labs and big publishers are fine, but they're a stopgap for the top hundred sites. The long tail needs something closer to a protocol: here are my terms, here's what I'll pay, settle automatically. That's what made ads work on the web. It wasn't that every site negotiated with every advertiser, it was that there was infrastructure in the middle.

Third, it has to make the economics work for the person actually creating. The reason I care about this is not nostalgia for publishers. If you don't fund the creation of new, high-quality information, the models have nothing fresh to learn from and nothing accurate to cite. You get a slow degradation where everything becomes a remix of what already exists. The pricing model is really a mechanism for keeping the supply of good content alive.

And fourth, it has to be legible to the model developers too. They need predictable costs and clear rights, otherwise they default to either hoarding what they've already scraped or litigating. Neither produces a healthy ecosystem.

My bet is that the thing that ends up working looks less like a paywall and more like a marketplace with real-time attribution and settlement. Content gets a price, agents decide whether it's worth paying, and the money flows based on actual contribution to the output. It's hard to build, mostly because attribution is genuinely a technical problem and not just a business one. But I'd rather solve that than watch the web fragment into a few giant licensed corpora and a lot of locked doors.

r001.rationale: The response discusses funding high-quality content, but does not clearly say that access prices should vary with the quality of the content accessed.

r002.rationale: It says payment should depend on downstream use and the content’s actual contribution to the output, rather than on crawling or fetching.

r003.rationale: It rejects bilateral deals as unworkable at scale and proposes a protocol with automatic terms and settlement.

r004.rationale: It discusses incentives and economic viability, but does not identify participants’ willingness to collaborate as the test of incentive alignment.

astra-6.text:
I think it needs to work for both sides. Publishers need a reason to make their content available, and AI developers need a predictable way to pay for it. If every interaction requires a separate negotiation, that’s going to be difficult to scale.

The tricky part is deciding what you’re pricing. Access for training is different from retrieving a page to answer a question in real time. And the value of that page can vary quite a bit depending on the question. So I wouldn’t assume there’s one price or one model that works everywhere.

I’d start with clear permissions, a way to measure usage, and a simple mechanism for payment. Then let people experiment. You need enough participation to learn what creates value for both the content owner and the application.

r001.rationale: The response says a page’s value can vary by question, but does not say pricing should vary with the quality of the content.

r002.rationale: It says the value of a page can vary depending on the question, conveying that the same content may be worth different amounts depending on the work performed with it.

r003.rationale: It says separate negotiations for every interaction would be difficult to scale and calls for a simple payment mechanism.

r004.rationale: It calls for enough participation to learn what creates value, but does not identify participants’ willingness to collaborate as the test of incentive alignment.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it needs to be simple enough that both sides can actually participate. Publishers need a reason to make their content available, and AI developers need predictable costs. If every website requires a separate negotiation, that’s going to work for a handful of very large companies and almost nobody else.

There’s also a distinction between using content to train a model and retrieving it to answer a question. Those are different uses, with different economics. I don’t think we should assume one price captures both.

A workable model needs a clear way to express permission, measure usage, and settle payments without adding a lot of friction. Then you can let prices evolve as people learn where the value is. We don’t yet know enough to design the perfect pricing model upfront.

r001.rationale: The response discusses different uses of content, but does not say pricing should vary with the quality of the content.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes training from retrieval and their economics, but does not state that pricing should vary with the value of the work performed using the same content.

r003.rationale: It rejects separate negotiations for every website as workable only for a few large companies and calls for low-friction permission, usage measurement, and payment settlement.

r004.rationale: It says the model should let both sides participate and give each incentives, but does not identify their willingness to collaborate as the test of incentive alignment.
